At Parque Cóndor above Otavalo, you can see birds of prey up close and learn how they are rescued. The centre occupies Pucará de Curiloma hill in the Ecuadorian Andes. From the grounds, visitors can see the Imbabura and Cotacachi volcanoes, so the walk among the birds comes with sweeping mountain views.

The park takes in birds rescued from illegal captivity or unsuitable conditions. Here they find shelter and a chance to recover; those whose condition allows it are prepared for release back into the wild. This story adds depth to meeting the centre's residents. Staff explanations help visitors see beyond the birds' beautiful plumage to their needs and the circumstances that led to their rescue.

One of the park's stars is the Andean condor. Its dark plumage, white ruff and powerful beak are easy to recognise even on a first encounter. Other birds of prey live at the centre too. During flight demonstrations, visitors can watch them spread their wings and manoeuvre through the air; these events depend on weather conditions.

Parque Cóndor fits naturally into a trip around Otavalo. After visiting the market and craft workshops, it is pleasant to turn your attention to the birds and mountain scenery. This is a stop for careful observation: studying feathers, following the movement of wings and hearing the story of a rescue. A visit offers an introduction to Andean wildlife and the people working to protect it.

It is especially rewarding to spend time with the brightly coloured birds here: some fly freely between branches, while others move along the ground and railings. During a visit, you can discover a variety of South American wildlife.

The park fits easily into a day exploring the Brazilian waterfalls. After the roar of the cascades, a walk through the greenery offers a chance to focus on the inhabitants of the tropical forest.

Visitors stop here to admire the Costa Verde coastline and the ocean horizon. Colourful ceramics and the flowing lines of the railings make the park a recognisable part of the waterfront.

The park features on city tours of Lima and provides a link between the capital's modern neighbourhoods and its historic centre. On the tour itinerary, it is a dedicated stop in Miraflores.

Under the trees, it is easy to forget the traffic on the neighbouring streets. The park has a rotunda, sculptures, a fountain and viewpoints, while its paths follow the natural changes in elevation. This combination of greenery and terrain distinguishes Lezama from many city squares.

The grounds are associated with the Lezama family, whose former home now houses the National Historical Museum. The park became a public space in the late 19th century. Nearby, on the other side of the street, you can see the blue domes of a Russian Orthodox church.

The park is ideal for a short walk while exploring San Telmo and the southern neighbourhoods of the capital. Visiting the museum and nearby churches is a separate choice from simply strolling through the green space.

The best way to experience the park is to walk along one of its lakes and watch the trees reflected in the water. Paths lead through different parts of the grounds, where locals stroll, exercise and relax in the shade.

Tres de Febrero opened in 1875. Its name refers to the Battle of Caseros, while the familiar name Bosques de Palermo points to the neighbourhood where the park is located. Carlos Thays later worked on its expansion. The rose garden, lakes and white bridge have become distinctive features of this space.

In and around the park are places to visit independently, including a planetarium and museums. A guided sightseeing tour covers the park as part of its route; individual attractions can be chosen according to your interests and available time.
